operationalization: Measure test height, diameter and plate thickness on vertical outlines of regular echinoids, fit each profile to a sessile-drop solution over a range of Bond numbers, and treat plate thickness as a proxy for shell tension. The claim would be supported if flattening increases as plate rigidity falls and the residuals match drop profiles; it would be weakened if spherical and flattened tests share the same plate thickness or if the outlines fit ellipses or cones as well as drops.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Digitized museum specimens and images of regular echinoids, including fossil and living tests, for vertical outline and height-to-diameter measurements

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and surface scans of biological specimens for three-dimensional test shape where echinoid tests have been imaged

obstacles: Open scans and profile photographs are sparse for flexible forms such as Phormosoma and for Palaeechinus.
Aristotle's lantern and apical buoyancy, which Thompson himself invoked for some outlines, are extra forces a single drop parameter does not absorb.
rationale: Drop profiles and a flattening index are standard geometric measurements, so the main series can be compared with an explicit physical family of shapes. Public images and scans cover only part of the regular echinoids, and plate-level mechanical properties are mostly in separate papers. A quantitative fit can still reject a pure drop model for the conical and collapsed forms, while agreement on the ordinary flattened series would remain compatible with several rounded geometries.

operationalization: Along arterial trees, regress wall thickness on lumen radius separately for large arteries and for small arteries and capillaries. Support would be a near-proportional relation in the large vessels and a clear drop in thickness-to-radius in the small ones; a single proportion across the whole size range, or walls that stay thick in capillaries, would refute the stated pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Cryosection cross-sections of human vessels from which wall thickness and radius can be measured in large and medium arteries

obstacles: Visible Human resolution does not reach capillary walls, and the claim's small-vessel limb depends on histology scattered through papers.
Elastic and muscular arteries differ in wall composition, so a single Laplace proportion is confounded by vessel class.
rationale: The decision rule is the Laplace scaling Thompson states: thickness tracks radius while pressure is roughly constant, then falls off as pressure drops. Open whole-body anatomy shows the large-vessel half of that pattern in humans. Capillaries and non-human vertebrates are poorly represented in downloadable volumes, so a full test across the stated scope still needs a histological compilation.

operationalization: From segmented cardiac surfaces, compute local wall thickness and mean curvature and test whether their product is constant within each chamber, with the left-ventricular apex the thinnest region. A flat thickness-curvature relation, or an apex as thick as the mid-wall, would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Open cardiac MRI with myocardial contours for mapping left-ventricular wall thickness against local curvature

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Anatomical cross-sections of the human heart for direct thickness measurements at the apex and free walls

obstacles: Open segmentations are dominated by the human left ventricle and under-sample the right ventricle, atria and other mammals.
Trabeculae, papillary muscles and the phase of the cardiac cycle change both thickness and curvature.
rationale: The inverse-curvature formula is explicit and cardiac MRI contours already support the regression in humans. That covers one mammal in detail and leaves the comparative scope thin. Partial-volume effects at the apex and the choice of which tissue counts as wall keep the test informative with a serious measurement confound.

operationalization: Estimate mean left-ventricular and right-ventricular wall thickness in the same hearts and compare their ratio with the ratio of systolic cavity pressures. The claim is confirmed if both ratios fall near 6-7 and match each other; a thickness ratio far from the pressure ratio, or either ratio far from 6-7, refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Cardiac MRI examinations and myocardial contours for left- versus right-ventricular wall thickness

obstacles: Ventricular pressure ratios are widely tabulated in clinical series and are weakly paired with the same open imaging files.
Where along the wall the thickness is taken changes the ratio.
rationale: Both halves of the claim are numerical, so a large human sample can confirm or reject the factor of six to seven. Open MRI supplies the thickness ratio directly, and published catheterization series supply the pressure ratio for the same species. Other mammals are less uniformly measured, but a systematic departure in humans would already refute the proportion as a general mammalian fact.

operationalization: On reconstructed arterial trees, compare observed radii, lengths and branching against the minimum-power, minimum-surface prediction (Murray scaling and short paths) and against alternatives such as space-filling or constant daughter-parent ratios. Support would be a lower combined cost than those rivals across beds; a consistent excess cost would refute the optimality claim.

candidate_datasets.name: BraVa
candidate_datasets.role: Reconstructions and morphometrics of human cerebral arterial trees for radii, lengths and branching cost

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Patient-specific vascular geometries and flow boundary conditions for comparing observed trees with minimum-work designs

obstacles: Effort can be operationalized as hydraulic power, wall surface, or endothelial shear, and those costs are not minimized by the same geometry.
Available trees are concentrated in the human brain and large vessels.
rationale: Downloadable arterial reconstructions contain the geometric variables an optimality test needs. Thompson's minimum of effort is broad enough that several cost functions remain compatible with the same trees, which is why discriminating power stays moderate. The data can reject crude nulls in humans and leave the vertebrate-wide claim only partly tested.

operationalization: At each bifurcation, measure the branch angle and the daughter-to-parent radius ratio. The claim is supported if angle declines as relative branch size increases, with the smallest side branches near 70-90 degrees and equal daughters leaving at equal angles; a flat or reversed angle-size relation would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BraVa
candidate_datasets.role: SWC reconstructions of human cerebral arteries with radii and bifurcation angles

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional models of human arteries outside the brain, for the same angle-versus-calibre regression

obstacles: Angles measured from projected angiograms differ from true three-dimensional angles.
Open trees sample humans heavily and leave most vertebrate groups unmeasured.
rationale: Roux's angle rules map onto radii and bifurcation angles that public vascular reconstructions already store. A small team can fit the angle-size curve and the equal-branch case with ordinary morphometry. Failure in these large human samples would refute the rule as a general arterial fact; agreement would establish it for the beds that dominate existing open data.

operationalization: For each branch, compare the observed angle with arccos of the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the parent and in the branch. Support would be a tight match between that predicted angle and the measured angle; systematic deviation toward a size-only or constant-angle rule would refute the energy-loss formula.

candidate_datasets.name: BraVa
candidate_datasets.role: Measured branch angles and radii from which a Poiseuille estimate of relative energy loss can be formed

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Geometries with flow boundary conditions and simulation outputs for a more direct estimate of dissipation along parent and branch

obstacles: Energy loss is usually inferred from radius and assumed flow, so the test can recycle the same hydraulic assumptions that motivate the formula.
Local pressure-drop measurements paired with angles are uncommon outside simulated models.
rationale: The cosine formula is explicit, and angles plus radii are in open reconstructions. Turning those radii into Thompson's energy loss per unit length requires a flow model, and Vascular Model Repository simulations cover only a subset of vessels. The resulting comparison can check consistency with the formula and struggles to separate it from other radius-based angle rules.

operationalization: The claim asserts that mechanical fitness of form can be demonstrated by statics and dynamics while cryptic, warning and mimetic colouration cannot. No measurement of organisms distinguishes that epistemic contrast from the rival view that both kinds of adaptation are demonstrable to similar standards.
obstacles: Demonstrability is a standard of evidence, and colour hypotheses and mechanical hypotheses fail or succeed under different criteria.
rationale: Biomechanical performance of fins or wings can be modelled, and those models do not decide whether colour explanations are undemonstrable. The sentence is a methodological ranking of kinds of argument. Existing performance datasets leave that ranking untouched.

operationalization: Compare ultimate tensile strength and compressive strength of fresh cortical bone, in kg per square mm, on matched specimens. The claim is confirmed if tension falls near 9-12, compression near 13-16, and the two are close; a large gap, or values far from those bands, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BoneMechDamage
candidate_datasets.role: Cyclic tensile stress-strain curves and fitted parameters for human femoral cortical bone and individual trabeculae

obstacles: Open files emphasize tensile tests of elderly human femoral bone; paired crushing tests of fresh bone across vertebrates are scattered in papers.
Dry, embalmed and demineralized specimens shift both strengths relative to fresh bone.
rationale: The numerical bands are a sharp decision rule. One open archive contains tensile curves for human femoral tissue and omits the matched crushing series Thompson quotes. A compilation of published material tests could finish the comparison for humans and a few other species, which is a real but partial test of fresh vertebrate bone.

operationalization: Measure the hollowness index (inner versus outer radius, or second-moment contribution of the cortex) in structures that carry bending in all directions and in structures loaded mainly in compression. Support would be thin-walled tubes in bird wing bones, quills and reed stems, and solid or thick-walled sections where bending is small; hollow compression members and solid bending members would refute the design rule.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT series of bird wing bones and other long bones for cortical thickness and medullary diameter

candidate_datasets.name: Odocoileus virginianus femur morphology and mechanics
candidate_datasets.role: Periosteal and endosteal diaphyseal diameters of fresh deer femora, a direct hollowness measurement for a weight-bearing bone

obstacles: Hollowness also serves marrow, pneumatization and mass reduction, so bending stiffness is not isolated by the cross-section alone.
Quills and reed stems are thinly represented beside vertebrate bone scans.
rationale: Cross-sectional geometry of long bones is measurable on open CT and on at least one tabulated femur series. Linking hollowness specifically to omnidirectional bending requires an independent load classification, and many hollow organs have other functions. The comparison can be run for bird wing bones versus some limb bones and remains a proxy for the full design claim, including plants and quills.

operationalization: Plot cortical thickness along the femoral shaft and compare it with the bending-moment diagram of a column loaded as the femur is loaded in stance. Support would be a midshaft maximum that tracks the moment and thins toward both ends; a proximal or distal maximum, or uniform walls, would refute the stated graph.

candidate_datasets.name: VSDFullBodyBoneReconstruction
candidate_datasets.role: Cadaver CT volumes and lower-limb segmentations for cortical thickness along the human femoral shaft

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Additional CT of femora and other weight-bearing long bones beyond the human cadaver series

obstacles: The moment diagram depends on whether the femur is treated as a simply loaded column, a cantilever, or a muscle-braced beam.
Muscle attachments and the calcar thicken the cortex locally, apart from the midshaft moment peak.
rationale: Open whole-femur CT is sufficient to test the descriptive claim that human femoral walls are thickest at midshaft and thin toward the ends. Matching that profile to a bending-moment graph requires a load model, and more than one plausible model moves the peak. The human femur, which is Thompson's central case, is therefore testable now, while the moment interpretation stays partly model-dependent.

operationalization: From micro-CT, extract trabecular orientations in the femoral head and compare them with principal-stress trajectories from a finite-element model of the same bone under stance loads, including a test that the two families cross near 90 degrees. Alignment well above a randomized or isotropic fabric would support the claim; a weak correlation or non-orthogonal crossings would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Edinburgh trabecular bone micro-CT
candidate_datasets.role: High-resolution micro-CT of trabecular cylinders for fabric orientation, as a microstructure source for stress-alignment tests

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Micro-CT of intact femoral heads, calcanei and tibiae where deposited, for comparing trabeculae with whole-bone stress trajectories

obstacles: Principal-stress directions change with the assumed joint loads, so a model can be tuned toward the anatomy.
Many open micro-CT volumes are excised cylinders rather than intact femoral heads under physiological boundary conditions.
rationale: Trabecular orientation and a finite-element stress map are both computable with existing methods, and some open micro-CT already resolves individual trabeculae. The classic crane comparison needs an intact loaded bone, which is less often deposited than small plugs. Because the stress field depends on boundary conditions that are not in the same files, agreement is informative and still open to circular loading assumptions.

operationalization: Track individual trabeculae through time under a known shear field and record whether oblique elements are displaced into the principal-stress directions while aligned elements stay put. Support would be shear-driven relocation on that time scale; loss and replacement by cell remodeling, with no displacement of the existing strut, would fail Thompson's mechanism even if the final pattern matches the stress lines.
obstacles: Static micro-CT shows the aligned end state and does not record whether shear moved the strut.
In-vivo loading series that do exist are small, scattered in papers, and rarely deposit the image time series.
rationale: The claim is a process, not the finished architecture. Public micro-CT can show that trabeculae end up aligned, which several mechanisms share. A decisive test needs longitudinal imaging of the same struts under controlled shear, and that kind of open time series is not available for the analysis Thompson's wording requires.

operationalization: In malunited fractures, compare trabecular orientation before injury and several weeks later with the principal-stress directions implied by the new alignment, including sites away from the fracture, and contrast those cases with fractures that heal in the original position. Wholesale realignment after displacement, and stability when alignment is unchanged, would support force-driven remodeling over a fixed hereditary pattern.
obstacles: Hospital CT series of malunion are rarely released as research datasets with trabecular resolution.
Published radiographs show selected cases and seldom quantify orientation far from the fracture over a defined number of weeks.
rationale: The prediction is empirically sharp: a changed load should rewrite the trabecular map within weeks, including away from the break. Clinical descriptions of that remodeling exist as case literature. They do not amount to an open, longitudinal, quantitative dataset on which a small team could confirm or refute the claim.

operationalization: Relate a measured increase in mechanical strain to a subsequent increase in tissue growth or thickness, with controls that hold hormones, perfusion and inflammation fixed. Support would be thicker bone, skin or supporting tissue under higher strain in those controls; growth that tracks systemic factors once strain is matched would fail the claim that strain itself is the direct stimulus.
obstacles: Loading experiments are numerous and scattered across papers, supplements and animal protocols rather than one open archive.
Surgical models such as tibial excision change blood flow and muscle use together with strain.
rationale: Strain versus later growth is measurable, and a large experimental literature already reports both. Calling the stimulus direct requires controls that most deposited tables do not include, and the public record is a compilation job rather than a single dataset. Existing studies can test the load-growth association in bone for a few species and leave skin, plants and the directness claim only partly constrained.

operationalization: Build arch, tied-arch and double-cantilever models on the same quadruped skeletal geometry and compare their horizontal thrust and moment diagrams with measured ground reaction forces and with the presence or absence of a ventral tie. The cantilever would be favoured if the limbs do not supply the arch's thrust and the spine's moments match a double-supported beam; a large horizontal thrust carried by the legs would favour the arch.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and surface scans of quadruped skeletons for vertebral and limb geometry used as the structural model

candidate_datasets.name: External mechanical work in the galloping racehorse
candidate_datasets.role: Force-plate records of forelimb and hindlimb loads in horses, as an empirical check on how the body is supported

obstacles: Muscles and ligaments act as time-varying ties, so a standing elastic analogy misses the dynamic case.
Open force data are concentrated on horses and a few other gait-lab species.
rationale: Skeletal geometry is openly scanned and horse ground reactions are deposited, so the rival structural models can be compared in a restricted set of quadrupeds. Ligament lines of action and material properties still have to be compiled. The exercise can reject a naive masonry arch for the horse and does not yet decide the analogy across standing quadrupeds.

operationalization: Measure neural-spine height at each vertebra and regress it on the bending moment predicted from body-segment masses and the positions of the limb supports. A positive proportional fit would support the claim; spine height that follows muscle size or display with no relation to the moment diagram would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebral-column scans from which neural-spine height can be measured along the trunk

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT slices of vertebrate skeletons for spine height relative to centrum size

obstacles: Segment masses and support points are only partly available in the same files as the skeletons.
Tall spines also anchor ligaments and epaxial muscles and, in some species, display structures.
rationale: Spine height is directly measurable on open CT once a bending-moment model is specified. That model is the cantilever picture of the preceding claim, so errors in mass distribution carry into the regression. A comparative sample can test proportionality in well-studied species and will confound mechanical moment with muscle attachment area.

operationalization: Sum vertical ground reactions on the forefeet and hindfeet of standing or slowly walking horses, elephants, camels and llamas and express the fore share of body weight. The claim is confirmed if horses and elephants fall near 55-58 percent and camels and llamas near two-thirds; shares near one-half, or a reversed ranking of those species, would refute the stated figures.

candidate_datasets.name: External mechanical work in the galloping racehorse
candidate_datasets.role: Open force-plate records giving forelimb versus hindlimb vertical impulse in Thoroughbreds during gallop

obstacles: The deposited horse series is a ridden gallop, whereas Thompson's percentages are for the standing load distribution.
Elephant, camel and llama force-plate tables are scattered in papers rather than one open archive.
rationale: The percentages are precise enough that force-plate data can settle them species by species. An open horse dataset exists and records a dynamic gait, so it speaks to load sharing without matching the standing condition. The other named species have published measurements that would have to be compiled before the full numerical claim can be confirmed or refuted.

operationalization: Across terrestrial vertebrates, relate the craniocaudal position of the tallest neural spines to the fraction of body mass in the head and neck versus the tail. Support would be withers spines where the head is heavy and lumbar or sacral spines where the tail is heavy or the animal is bipedal; a single spinal peak unrelated to that mass distribution would refute the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Skeletal scans of living and fossil vertebrates for neural-spine profiles and relative head, neck and tail size

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT of additional skeletons for the same spine-height and mass-distribution comparison

obstacles: Fossil body-mass fractions are estimated from the skeleton itself, which couples the predictor to the measurement.
Display spines and phylogeny can produce tall withers in light-headed species.
rationale: Spine profiles and rough mass distribution are recoverable from open skeletal scans for many of the living and fossil cases Thompson names. The prediction is comparative and can be fit with phylogenetic regression. Uncertainty in fossil masses and non-mechanical uses of tall spines keep the test from cleanly isolating bending moment.

operationalization: Compare relative neural-spine height over the withers and haunches in whales, seals and sirenians with that of their terrestrial relatives, and compare pelvic depth and curvature in aquatic versus terrestrial birds. The claim is supported if the tall arched spines and deep pelves are absent in the aquatic forms after body size and phylogeny are accounted for; retention of those peaks in fully aquatic species would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT scans of cetaceans, pinnipeds, sirenians and birds for vertebral-spine and pelvic proportions

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Additional skeletal CT of aquatic and terrestrial vertebrates for the same contrast

obstacles: Aquatic clades share ancestry, so a phylogenetic comparative model is required.
Museum scans over-represent a few well-studied genera within each marine group.
rationale: The morphological contrast is large and the named groups are present in open CT libraries. Spine height and pelvic shape can be measured with standard landmarks and compared with terrestrial relatives under a phylogenetic model. That is enough for a small team to confirm or refute the claimed loss, with uneven sampling inside each clade as the main limit.

operationalization: On vertebrae of round-bodied fishes such as cod and haddock, and on whale vertebrae, measure the angles among the neural spine and the two transverse processes. The geometric claim is supported if those angles cluster near 120 degrees; a strong departure toward a different symmetric or asymmetric arrangement would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT of fish and cetacean vertebrae for angles among the neural and transverse processes

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Slice data on fish skeletons for the same angular measurement

obstacles: Angles are not pre-tabulated and must be measured from scans that are uneven across ordinary round-bodied fishes.
The further claim that 120 degrees maximizes uniform stiffness needs a separate mechanical model of the ligament system.
rationale: The 120-degree arrangement is a direct angular measurement on existing vertebral CT. Coverage is good enough for a sample of fishes and some whales and is not yet a survey of round-bodied fishes. The stiffness-maximizing interpretation can be checked with a simple structural model once the angles are in hand, so the geometric half of the claim is the part current scans can settle.

operationalization: Compare vertebral depth-to-span ratios of large vertebrates with the depth an engineering cantilever of similar load would use, and test whether shallower columns are more flexible under the same material. A large, consistent shortfall in depth together with a flexibility gain would support the claim; depths inside the engineering range, or no link between depth and flexibility, would undermine it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Skeletal scans, including large fossil vertebrates, for depth-to-length ratios of the vertebral girder

obstacles: What an engineer would build depends on the allowable stress, safety factor and load case, none of which Thompson fixes.
Shallow spines also follow development and phylogeny, so flexibility is hard to isolate as the reason.
rationale: Depth-to-length of a backbone is measurable on open scans, including some of the large animals named in the text. The reference cantilever and the requirement for flexibility are only loosely specified, so many observed depths can be reconciled with the claim. The data support a descriptive comparison and do not cleanly establish the functional reason.

operationalization: Quantify, from trabeculae up to whole-skeleton layout, the fraction of bony material aligned with computed principal stresses, and set a threshold for 'a very large extent'. The claim would be supported only if that fraction is high at both scales across vertebrates; alignment confined to a few bones, or a low fraction once loads are fixed in advance, would refute the global wording.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT from bone microstructure to whole skeletons for stress-alignment comparisons

candidate_datasets.name: Edinburgh trabecular bone micro-CT
candidate_datasets.role: Trabecular volumes for the microstructural end of the same comparison

obstacles: The phrase 'a very large extent' has no numerical cutoff, so many partial alignments count as success.
Stress maps and the skeleton that is supposed to diagram them are often inferred from the same geometry.
rationale: Pieces of the claim, especially trabecular and long-bone alignment, can be tested with existing scans. The sentence itself sums every level of the skeleton into one unquantified tendency. Those datasets can support or weaken local versions and leave the global claim without a single confirming or refuting result.

operationalization: Using molecular or other independent trees as the reference, compare phylogenetic signal and homoplasy of scapulae and vertebrae with that of other skeletal characters, especially in lineages that changed habitat. The claim is supported if those mechanically loaded bones mislead more often than other characters; equal or higher reliability would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogeny as an independent reference against which skeletal characters can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published morphological matrices containing scapular, vertebral and other skeletal characters

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Scans of scapulae and vertebrae for measuring shape convergence among animals with similar habits

obstacles: Extinct test cases such as Zeuglodon have no genome, so the reference tree is itself partly morphological.
Character coding and missing fossils change apparent homoplasy.
rationale: Independent trees and morphological matrices exist, so homoplasy of single bones can be compared with other characters in living vertebrates. That is a fair proxy for 'unreliable as evidence of blood-relationship'. The fossil illustration cannot be checked with molecules, and habitat-linked convergence is only partly separated from coding decisions.

operationalization: After habitat or locomotor shifts, measure whether shape change is spread in a graded way across many skeletal regions or concentrated in single bones. Support would be higher morphological integration and more spatially graded change in those transitions than in single-element outliers; a record of isolated, bone-by-bone changes would refute the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Multi-element skeletal scans for measuring correlated shape change across body regions

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic backbone for comparing lineages that changed habitat or posture

obstacles: Developmental pleiotropy produces correlated change whether or not new mechanical forces are the cause.
Fossil sequences rarely preserve enough associated elements to separate graded change from sampling gaps.
rationale: Integration of shape across skeletal parts is a standard analysis on open scans and trees. The claim adds that new mechanical forces are what produce the graded pattern, and integration studies also match developmental correlation. Current data can document coordinated change and cannot isolate the mechanical cause.

operationalization: The claim says living forms differ from mathematical ideals only in the way inorganic forms do, because secondary forces are always present. Any measured deviation can be assigned to some secondary force, so no dataset result separates the claim from a view that organisms depart from ideals for distinct biological reasons.
obstacles: The ideal figure and the secondary forces are chosen after the form is seen.
rationale: The sentence denies an essential difference between organic and inorganic form and explains every departure by unspecified extra forces. Shape archives can measure deviation from a chosen ideal and cannot show that the deviation has the same kind of cause as a sagging chain or an imperfect raindrop. The claim stays conceptual.

operationalization: Within genera or classes, partition species differences into relative magnitudes (uniform scaling, shear and simple gradients) versus discrete, localized novelties. The claim is supported if most between-species shape distance lies in the proportional part; a large share of discrete character changes would refute 'mainly'.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional specimens of related species for geometric morphometric partitions of shape difference

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices that record discrete differences alongside continuous proportions

obstacles: What counts as the main cause depends on whether landmarks or presence-absence characters are given priority.
Well-sampled clades are a minority of classes and genera.
rationale: Relative magnitude versus discrete novelty can be scored with existing scans and matrices for some groups. 'Main cause of specific differences' still needs a threshold and a choice of characters, and both choices move the result. The data can show that proportions dominate in particular clades and cannot underwrite the general causal wording.

operationalization: Fit related species with a low-dimensional coordinate transformation of the whole body and with a model of independent regional changes, and compare held-out landmark error. A large advantage for the global transformation would support an integrated law of growth; the morphological fit would still leave natural selection unrefuted unless selection is separately shown to require part-by-part independence.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Comparable scans of related species for whole-body versus regional shape models

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs and morphometrics of related fishes for outline-level tests of global versus local difference

obstacles: A good global fit is also what selection on an integrated phenotype would produce.
Thompson's rival, independent variation of separate parts, is a historical picture of selection rather than a distinct morphological null.
rationale: Whole-body transformations versus modular shape change can be compared on open images and scans. That tests the pattern half of the claim. It does not test the historical assertion that the pattern rules out natural selection, because selection is compatible with correlated change across the body.

operationalization: For pairs of related species, compare held-out landmark error of a simple symmetrical map (affine, shear, or a low-order coordinate stretch) with a high-parameter warp. The claim is supported if the simple map is usually enough across fishes, crustaceans and skulls; frequent need for localized warps would refute 'as a general rule'.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Cross-taxon 3D specimens for fitting simple versus complex transformations between related species

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT of fishes, reptiles and mammals for the same paired-species test

obstacles: Simplicity is a continuous property, so the cutoff for a 'simple' map has to be chosen.
Published scans over-represent a few clades relative to the full range of classes Thompson cites.
rationale: The theory of transformations is directly testable as a model-comparison problem on existing specimens. Open archives support that test for many pairs and fall short of a balanced sample of every class he has in view. Results would show how often a simple map suffices in the sampled groups, which is a partial answer to a claim about the general rule.

operationalization: For fossils from folded strata, compare shape differences with an independent tectonic strain estimate and ask whether names later treated as separate species collapse once that shear is removed. Support would be repeated cases where the residual biological difference is within species-level variation; persistent differences after retrodeformation would count against mistaking shear for taxonomy.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic names, occurrences and localities that can be matched to deformed rock units before strain and synonymy are compiled from other sources

obstacles: Strain markers and the taxonomic histories of supposed species are scattered by locality, not stored with the occurrence data.
Biological variation and compaction can mimic tectonic shear.
rationale: The claim is a countable historical pattern: sheared fossils have often been named as separate species. Occurrence databases list candidate taxa and localities, while the strain measurements and later synonymies live in local geological papers. A team can assemble a partial test for well-studied slates and cannot yet survey deformed strata in general.

operationalization: Scale ox, sheep and giraffe cannon bones to equal length and compare breadth, then inspect residual shape after a single transverse stretch. The claim is confirmed if sheep breadth is about two-thirds and giraffe breadth about one-third of the ox, with little residual shape difference; substantially different ratios, or large residuals at the ends and shaft, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of ruminant metapodials for length, breadth and residual shape after a one-axis stretch

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen photographs and records of ox, sheep and giraffe cannon bones for the same ratios across individuals

obstacles: Breed, sex and age change metapodial proportions within domestic ox and sheep.
Giraffe samples in open archives are smaller than livestock samples.
rationale: The claimed ratios are numerical and the bones are ordinary museum objects with scans and photographs available. A one-axis scaling leaves a residual that can be tested directly against a more complex shape difference. Within-species variation is the main caveat, and it is measurable in the same specimens.

operationalization: Measure radial and tangential growth velocities on developing dicot leaves, or, as a weaker proxy, test whether a single ratio of those velocities carries mature outlines from lanceolate through ovate to cordate. Support would be that ordered continuum in the growth data; outlines that require a changing ratio or a different growth centre would refute the mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Herbarium images of dicot leaves spanning lanceolate, ovate and cordate outlines for the geometric proxy

obstacles: Pressed outlines do not record growth velocities, which are the variables the mechanism names.
Time-lapse and clonal-analysis datasets exist for a few model species and are not a dicot-wide archive.
rationale: Mature leaf silhouettes are abundant and can show whether one geometric parameter orders the named shapes. The claim is about velocities of radial and tangential growth, and those velocities are rarely deposited. Outline fits are a proxy that several growth rules can satisfy.

operationalization: On begonia leaves, measure angles from the base to corresponding radii on each side of the midrib and test whether those angles stay in a constant ratio. A stable ratio, mapping an ovate half onto a cordate half, would support unequal similar growth; a ratio that changes along the midrib would show true asymmetry and refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Digitized herbarium sheets and photographs of Begonia leaves for bilateral radial measurements

obstacles: Pressing and mounting distort angles, especially in thin cordate lobes.
Species and leaf position on the plant add biological scatter around a single ratio.
rationale: The constant-proportion prediction is a simple measurement on leaf images, and Begonia is widely digitized. A varying angle ratio is a direct refutation, and a stable ratio across many leaves is positive evidence. Mounting distortion is a real bias and can be checked by comparing pressed sheets with photographs of fresh leaves in the same portal.

operationalization: The claim says organisms grow along stream lines of a suitable transformation, with non-orthogonal cases explained by inhomogeneity. Because the transformation is chosen to fit the growth, every smooth growth field satisfies the description, and no public dataset can separate it from a rival growth law.
obstacles: Cell-tracking volumes exist for a few model embryos and still leave the transformation free to be chosen afterward.
rationale: Stream lines are a redescription of whatever displacement field the organism shows once a coordinate map has been fitted. Departures from orthogonality are assigned to the tissue not being homogeneous. That structure has no measurable outcome that would count against the claim.

operationalization: For organs such as the stomach, heart and gut, test whether shape matches a pressure vessel of uniform expansion plus localized constraints such as a muscular band, using the unconstrained vessel as the rival. Agreement at the named constrictions would support those examples; shapes that miss the constraint prediction would limit how many organs the account covers.

candidate_datasets.name: Visible Human Project
candidate_datasets.role: Cross-sectional anatomy of gut, stomach and heart for comparing adult form with a constrained pressure-vessel model

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Heart shape data for the cardiac example of constrained expansion

obstacles: Adult shape is compatible with many developmental histories, so a geometric match does not show that growth was uniform expansion under a trammel.
The word 'many' sets no quota of organs that must fit.
rationale: Particular illustrations, such as a banded stomach or a lobed heart, can be compared with images of adult organs. The claim is about the developmental process that produced them, and static anatomy is only a proxy. Because constraints can be placed after the fact, a fit does little to separate this account from other growth rules.

operationalization: Landmark outlines and homologous external points of Diodon and Mola, fit one low-parameter transformation of the sort Thompson drew, and score held-out points, including whether the head stays nearly unmoved. The claim is supported if that single map predicts the held-out anatomy; a need for separate local warps of body regions would refute the integral-transformation account.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs and species records of Diodon and Mola for outline and landmark comparison

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen scans, where deposited, for three-dimensional homologous points beyond the silhouette

obstacles: A sufficiently flexible warp can map any two outlines, so the test has to freeze a simple transformation and hold landmarks out.
Individual and preservational variation in these deep-bodied fishes adds scatter around one diagrammatic map.
rationale: The claim is about two named forms, both of which are extensively photographed and present in museum collections. A pre-specified simple map with held-out landmarks is a standard test and can fail. That makes the external-transformation claim resolvable with existing images, with the usual caution that outline agreement is weaker than agreement of internal landmarks.

operationalization: Landmark crocodilian skulls, including individual bones and vacuities, fit one simple coordinate map from Crocodylus to other genera, and test whether the map reconstructs Notosuchus bone for bone on held-out landmarks. Support would be low error across most genera; large residuals in particular bones or in Notosuchus would refute the single-deformation account.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT of crocodilian skulls for bone-by-bone landmarks and fenestrae

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Additional living and fossil crocodilian crania, including specimens closer to Notosuchus where scanned

obstacles: Fossil crushing mimics coordinate deformation.
Open scans cover living crocodilians more densely than the fossil genera needed for a bone-for-bone reconstruction of Notosuchus.
rationale: Living crocodilian skulls are available as CT, so a single-map model can be tested against mosaic change in snout, vault and vacuities. The stronger claim, that Notosuchus can be rebuilt bone for bone from Crocodylus, depends on fossil specimens whose open 3D coverage is thinner and whose distortion is a serious confound. Existing data can settle much of the living comparison and only part of the fossil reconstruction.

operationalization: Place Perissodactyla, other ungulates, Leporidae and other rodents on genome-based trees and test the two sister-group claims: perissodactyls closer to rabbits than to other ungulates, and rabbits closer to perissodactyls than to other rodents. Either grouping is refuted if the credible trees put perissodactyls with other laurasiatheres and rabbits with rodents.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogeny of mammals for the perissodactyl-lagomorph relationship

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Compiled published divergence times and trees for the same clades

obstacles: Deep mammal nodes still differ in a few published studies, though the Glires versus Laurasiatheria split is repeatedly recovered.
The skull-flexure argument that motivated the claim is a separate morphological question and is not settled by the tree alone.
rationale: The claim is a phylogenetic hypothesis about named living clades, and those clades are densely sampled in public trees built from molecular data independent of the skull transformation. A small team can read the relationship off existing syntheses in days. That is a direct confirm-or-refute test of the relatedness statement.

operationalization: Build a coordinate path from Hyracotherium to Equus and measure the distance of Mesohippus and Protohippus skulls to the interpolated shapes, relative to skulls that are not on that path. Close coincidence, closer than off-path equids, would support the claim; distances as large as those of unrelated perissodactyls would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Scans of fossil and living equid skulls where museums have deposited them

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic and occurrence framework for which equid skulls exist to be measured

obstacles: Complete, undistorted skulls of the named fossil genera are few, and only some are openly scanned.
A linear morph between two endpoints can pass near intermediate fossils without those fossils lying on the phylogenetic path.
rationale: The interpolation test is well defined and the taxa are classical, with published measurements and a growing set of scans. Open 3D coverage of Mesohippus, Protohippus and Hyracotherium is incomplete, so a team would still compile plates and specimens. The geometric coincidence can be assessed for the available skulls and does not by itself prove the phylogenetic series.

operationalization: Place Parahippus on the same Hyracotherium-to-Equus morph and on a cladogram of equids built from characters other than the interpolated skull warp. The claim is supported if Parahippus is both a poor geometric fit and sits off the Equus stem; a good fit, or a stem position despite a poor fit, would separate the geometric evidence from the phylogenetic conclusion.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Equid cranial scans for the geometric distance of Parahippus from the interpolated series

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence and taxonomic context for Parahippus and the other equid genera in the comparison

obstacles: A poor fit to a linear warp can reflect age, sex or crushing rather than a side branch.
Equid phylogeny is morphological, so the tree and the skull transformation share character evidence.
rationale: Parahippus skulls and equid phylogenies exist in the literature and, unevenly, as scans. The logical step from 'fits the picture poorly' to 'not on the direct line' needs independent characters, which only partly exist for an extinct genus. Current material can test the geometric half and leaves the phylogenetic conclusion underdetermined.

operationalization: Compare human, chimpanzee and baboon skulls with one continuous transformation and test whether corresponding grid areas increase approximately logarithmically downward and forward. Support would be a single smooth gradient that predicts held-out landmarks; a better fit from separate jaw, face and braincase modules would refute the one-process account.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D crania of humans, chimpanzees and baboons for a continuous versus modular deformation

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT of anthropoid skulls for the same landmark comparison

obstacles: Size-related allometry can look logarithmic without being a single developmental deformation.
Landmark choice on the face versus the vault changes how continuous the gradient appears.
rationale: The three skulls are heavily archived as CT and surface scans, and the logarithmic, one-process prediction is a concrete model comparison against modular alternatives. A small team can run that comparison with standard geometric morphometrics. Allometry and landmark scheme are real confounds and do not block a decisive test.

operationalization: Ask whether one transformation series can be drawn through Mesopithecus, Homo erectus (Pithecanthropus), Neanderthals and modern humans with lower error than a branching arrangement of the same skulls. A large advantage for the branching model would support divergent change; a single series that passes through the fossils in order would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Scans of fossil and living hominid and anthropoid crania where repositories have released them

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Additional primate cranial CT for the living end of the comparison

obstacles: Key fossils are few, often reconstructed, and unevenly available for download.
Which specimens are admitted as successive stages changes whether a straight series appears to fail.
rationale: The absence of a single straight series is a testable geometric claim, and many of the relevant crania have been measured or scanned. Open access and reconstruction choices are uneven for Pithecanthropus and Neanderthals especially. Existing material can reject some linear stories and cannot yet treat the full fossil sample as a clean public dataset.

operationalization: Across related fishes, test whether body depth and body width vary inversely and whether the length-weight coefficient k = W/L^3 changes less than either linear ratio, including the specific claim that plaice is about twice as deep and half as thick as haddock at similar k. An inverse depth-width relation with stable k would support the claim; independent depth and width, or a large k difference for that pair, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Length-weight coefficients and available body-depth records for haddock, plaice and other related fishes

obstacles: Body width is recorded far less often than length-weight parameters, so the inverse-compensation half is data-limited.
Length type and seasonal condition shift k independently of the depth-width tradeoff.
rationale: FishBase already holds the length-weight half of the claim for thousands of species, including the named pair, and a k comparison is immediate. The inverse relation between depth and thickness needs body width, which the same database covers only patchily. The volume-conservation statement is testable now for many species, and the full geometric tradeoff is testable only where both transverse dimensions were published.

operationalization: The claim says a mathematical treatment is essential to understanding organic form. Essentiality is a judgment about method, and no measurement of organisms would confirm or refute it.
obstacles: Success or failure of particular mathematical descriptions does not decide whether mathematics is essential to morphology.
rationale: This is a closing statement about what morphologists ought to use. Datasets can illustrate particular regularities of form. They have no decision criterion for whether a mathematical aspect is essential to the science.

operationalization: The claim identifies whatever is most beautiful and regular in natural form with whatever is most useful. Beauty and regularity are not fixed measured variables, so no dataset can show that the most regular forms are the most useful across nature generally.
obstacles: A special case such as the honeycomb can be studied mechanically without giving the universal wording a decision criterion.
rationale: The epilogue asserts a general coincidence of mathematical beauty and usefulness, with the bee's cell as an illustration. Usefulness can be defined for particular structures. The universal identification of the most beautiful with the most useful has no measurable contrast that would refute it.

operationalization: The claim says living and non-living things are governed by the same physical and mathematical laws. Without a specified law and a specified violation, no dataset distinguishes this from a rival that reserves some biological phenomena for other principles.
obstacles: Any particular biophysical success confirms only that case, and the sentence names no case.
rationale: This is a general metaphysical commitment of the book. Particular physical relations elsewhere in the text can be tested with data. The epilogue sentence itself names no variable and no outcome that would count as confirmation or refutation.
